How the model structure is chosen

pdmS7 documentation

Source: vignettes/choosing-structure.Rmd
choosing-structure.Rmd

The structure of a model, its soil store, recharge rule and routing, is a modelling decision like any other, and a reviewer may ask why this one. “It is the standard” is an answer; “we calibrated the alternatives alike and this one did best on data the calibration never saw” is a better one. compare_structures() gives that answer, and logs it.

This article first explains how recommend_structure() chooses the soil store, recharge rule and groundwater store, step by step. It then compares eight structures on a synthetic catchment whose true structure is known, and carries the chosen one through validation and a final test. The component guide explains what each component does.

How the structure is chosen

recommend_structure() chooses the structure one component at a time, as a hydrologist would, and writes down why. calibrate_project(recommend = TRUE) calls it before the staged calibration. Each step changes one component and holds the others at what the steps before chose:

Step Component Options compared
1 Recharge rule standard, split, demand
2 Soil store distribution Pareto, rectangular, triangular, exponential, lognormal
3 Groundwater store cubic, quadratic, linear, exponential

Why this order. It follows what a record can tell apart. On made-up catchments whose true structure is known (What automatic calibration recovers), the recharge rule was identified every time, by margins of 0.08 or more in log NSE, and the groundwater store only by margins too small to trust. Deciding the clearest question first means the later, harder choices are made on a structure that is already right where the record can say so.

What each step does. Every option is calibrated alike, by compare_structures(): the same objective, starts, seed and iteration limit, bounds from calibration_bounds() for its own components, on the calibration window. Each is then scored on the validation window, which no calibration saw. One rule then makes the choice:

  1. Set aside any option bent to fit. An option that ended with a parameter at a bound of its search range is not describing the catchment; the search pushed it as far as it could go. It is set aside, unless every option did. (Split recharge cannot end at a share of 0 or 1, which would switch a flow path off: its search range is 0.05 to 0.95.)
  2. Find the equally good. Every remaining option within the tie tolerance of the best validation score counts as equally good: 0.02 in NSE unless the project registered another. A smaller difference is a tie, not a result; another seed or another winter could reorder them.
  3. Keep the current component if it is among them. The record cannot justify a change. This makes the recommendation conservative: where the record is silent, as it usually is about the groundwater store, the standard structure stays.
  4. Otherwise, break the tie on the floods. Among the equally good, the option with the smallest median peak error on the largest validation events wins, then the one with fewer parameters.

An example. On one catchment the groundwater step compared:

Option Parameters Calibration NSE Validation NSE
exponential 8 0.9362 0.9172
quadratic 7 0.9387 0.9171
linear 7 0.9165 0.8923
cubic (current) 7 0.8826 0.8369

The exponential and quadratic stores are equally good, 0.0001 apart. The current cubic store is not among them, 0.08 behind, so rule 3 does not keep it. Rule 4 chose the exponential store for its smaller median peak error on the largest validation floods. Had their peak errors been equal, the quadratic store would have won on fewer parameters.

Every comparison is logged, and each step’s choice and reason is written as a note, so the recommendation is part of the audit trail:

rec <- recommend_structure(project, reasoning = "First choice of structure.")
rec                           # one line per step: choice and reason
rec$steps$recharge$table      # the comparison, with at_bound and equally_good

Zones, if asked. With zones = c(1, 2) in calibrate_project(), a fourth step compares the structure chosen as one zone with the same structure plus a small fast zone, by the same rule (Choosing model components; worked through in The two-zone PDM). Use it where one PDM cannot give a sharp spike and a slower flood hydrograph at once: the signs are a split recharge share at its lower bound and surface stores at their caps in every fit.

What it does not choose. The surface routing stays a cascade of two linear stores, the standard and almost always adequate. The groundwater extension is not tried automatically: it needs abstraction data or a reason to expect losses, and its parameters cannot be pinned down from flow alone. Add it to the configuration when the catchment calls for it (Choosing model components).

The rest of this article runs a full comparison by hand, on a made-up catchment, and carries the chosen structure through validation and a final test.

The catchment

The “true” catchment has a lognormal soil store. The calibrator is not told.

set.seed(11)
n <- 24 * 75
time <- seq(as.POSIXct("2023-10-01", tz = "UTC"), by = 3600, length.out = n)
forcing <- data.frame(
  time = time, pet = 0.06,
  rain = ifelse(stats::runif(n) < 0.07, stats::rgamma(n, 0.7, scale = 3), 0)
)
truth <- structure_set("lognormal")$lognormal
truth$area_km2 <- 60
truth$fc <- 1.1
truth$distribution$meanlog <- 4.8
truth$distribution$sdlog <- 0.5
truth$recharge$kg <- 2000
truth$surface$k1 <- 3
truth$surface$k2 <- 10
# The river is already flowing when the record starts: steady state, not empty stores.
truth_model <- pdm_from_config(truth)
observed <- run_pdm(truth_model, forcing,
                    initial_state_from_flow(truth_model, 1, 0.7))$output$q_m3s *
  exp(stats::rnorm(n, 0, 0.04))

The project registers three windows: calibration, validation, and a final test window. Ranking structures on the validation window uses it up as an independent check, so the test window is kept back, scored once, at the end, by nothing but test_candidate().

options(pdmS7.user = "Ann Hydrologist", pdmS7.role = "custodian")
project <- file.path(tempdir(), "structure-choice")
start_calibration_project(project, catchment = "Example Brook", gauge = "99002",
                          purpose = "Structure selection", area_km2 = 60,
                          owner = "Deputy Director", steward = "Sam Steward")
reg <- register_data(project, forcing, observed,
                     calibration = c("2023-10-08", "2023-11-20"),
                     validation = c("2023-11-21", "2023-12-05"),
                     test = c("2023-12-06", "2023-12-14"), wettest_years = 0)

The candidates

structure_set() gives the standard PDM and seven variants, each one change from it, so each comparison answers one question.

structures <- structure_set()
data.frame(
  structure = names(structures),
  soil = vapply(structures, function(s) s$distribution$type, ""),
  recharge = vapply(structures, function(s) s$recharge$type, ""),
  groundwater = vapply(structures, function(s) s$groundwater$type, ""),
  row.names = NULL
)
#>                 structure        soil recharge groundwater
#> 1                standard      pareto standard       cubic
#> 2             rectangular rectangular standard       cubic
#> 3              triangular  triangular standard       cubic
#> 4             exponential exponential standard       cubic
#> 5               lognormal   lognormal standard       cubic
#> 6                   split      pareto    split       cubic
#> 7                  demand      pareto   demand       cubic
#> 8 exponential_groundwater      pareto standard exponential

Each structure calibrates the parameters of its own components, within bounds from a table shipped with the package. Parameters that span orders of magnitude are searched on a log scale, so that a recharge constant of 10 hours gets as much attention as one of 1,000.

calibration_bounds(structures$lognormal)[, c("path", "lower", "upper", "scale")]
#>                   path lower   upper  scale
#> 1 distribution.meanlog   2.3       6 linear
#> 2   distribution.sdlog   0.1       2 linear
#> 3          recharge.kg   1.0    5000    log
#> 4           surface.k1   0.5      72    log
#> 5           surface.k2   0.5      72    log
#> 6       groundwater.kb 100.0 1000000    log

Bounds can be overridden for a catchment you know, with overrides, or a parameter held fixed with exclude. The rainfall factor fc is held at its configured value unless an override gives it bounds. This made-up catchment’s rain is known to be 10 per cent low, so the comparison below unlocks it.

The comparison

Every structure gets the same objective, starts, seed and iteration limit. With cores, the structures run in parallel; here they run in turn.

elapsed <- system.time(
  ranking <- compare_structures(project, structures, starts = 2, control = list(maxit = 30),
                                overrides = list(fc = c(0.6, 1.6)),
                                reasoning = "Which structure suits this catchment?")
)[["elapsed"]]
round(elapsed)
#> [1] 48
ranking[, .(rank, structure, parameters, calibration = round(calibration, 4),
            validation = round(validation, 4), change = round(change, 4), starts_agree)]
#>     rank               structure parameters calibration validation  change
#>    <int>                  <char>      <int>       <num>      <num>   <num>
#> 1:     1               lognormal          7      0.9962     0.9952 -0.0010
#> 2:     2                   split          7      0.9861     0.9942  0.0082
#> 3:     3                standard          7      0.9958     0.9895 -0.0062
#> 4:     4 exponential_groundwater          8      0.9957     0.9879 -0.0078
#> 5:     5             rectangular          6      0.9950     0.9844 -0.0107
#> 6:     6             exponential          6      0.9916     0.9795 -0.0121
#> 7:     7                  demand          9      0.9445     0.9276 -0.0169
#> 8:     8              triangular          6      0.9198     0.8929 -0.0270
#>    starts_agree
#>          <lgcl>
#> 1:        FALSE
#> 2:         TRUE
#> 3:         TRUE
#> 4:        FALSE
#> 5:        FALSE
#> 6:        FALSE
#> 7:        FALSE
#> 8:        FALSE
k <- nrow(ranking)
par(mar = c(4, 12, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(NA, xlim = range(c(ranking$calibration, ranking$validation)), ylim = c(0.5, k + 0.5),
     yaxt = "n", xlab = "NSE", ylab = "")
axis(2, at = k:1, labels = ranking$structure, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.85)
segments(ranking$calibration, k:1, ranking$validation, k:1, col = pal[7])
points(ranking$calibration, k:1, pch = 1, col = pal[1], cex = 1.3)
points(ranking$validation, k:1, pch = 16, col = pal[1], cex = 1.3)

Calibration (open) and validation (filled) NSE for each structure, best on validation at the top.

Reading the ranking

The true structure, lognormal, ranks first. It would be wrong to conclude much from that alone: 2 structures lie within 0.005 NSE of the top on validation, a spread of 9.7^{-4}. A difference that small is a tie, not a result; another seed or another few weeks of data could reorder them.

At the other end, demand and triangular trail the top by more than 0.05 NSE on validation. A gap that size is a conclusion the data do support: on this catchment, those structures should not be chosen.

Three things to read in any comparison:

  • The spread at the top. Differences smaller than the noise between starts or between years are ties. Longer records, including a dry summer, separate soil stores; a few weeks cannot.
  • The change from calibration to validation. A structure that gains in calibration and loses in validation is fitting noise with its extra parameters.
  • Whether the starts agreed. Where they did not, as for lognormal, exponential_groundwater, rectangular, exponential, demand, triangular, the structure may have been under-calibrated; give it more starts or iterations before ruling it out.

Faced with a tie, prefer the simplest structure, the one with fewest parameters, among those within a stated margin of the best. Stating the margin in advance keeps the choice honest.

margin <- 0.005
tied <- ranking[validation >= ranking$validation[1] - margin]
choice <- tied[order(parameters, rank)][1]
choice[, .(structure, parameters, validation = round(validation, 4), calibration_entry)]
#>    structure parameters validation calibration_entry
#>       <char>      <int>      <num>            <char>
#> 1: lognormal          7     0.9952              0012

Validation and the final test

The chosen calibration becomes the candidate, is validated, and then, with structure and parameters fixed, is tested once on the window nobody has looked at.

propose_candidate(project, entry = choice$calibration_entry,
                  reasoning = paste("Simplest structure within", margin,
                                    "NSE of the best on validation."))
validate_candidate(project, "Validation as in the comparison.")
final <- test_candidate(project, "Final check on held-back data.")
round(c(calibration = final$calibration_scores$nse,
        validation = final$validation_scores$nse, test = final$test_scores$nse), 4)
#> calibration  validation        test 
#>      0.9962      0.9952      0.9939

The test score is the honest estimate of how the chosen model will do on new data, because nothing was chosen with it. A Steward cannot sign off a project with a test window until the test has been run, and sees all three scores side by side in the report.

Cross-validation

With a short record, one validation window is a thin basis for a ranking. cross_validate = TRUE also calibrates each structure on the validation window and scores it on the calibration window, and ranks on the mean of the two held-out scores. It doubles the cost.

compare_structures(project, structures, starts = 4, cross_validate = TRUE, cores = 8,
                   reasoning = "Short record: rank on both held-out windows.")

In the app and at scale

The app’s Structures tab runs the same comparison: tick the structures, set the starts and cores, and press the button. Every comparison is logged, structure_comparison() rebuilds its ranking from the log at any time, and the report includes it.

Across many catchments, the question becomes which structure wins most often, and by how much. Combine this article with Calibrating many catchments:

winners <- vapply(folders, function(f) {
  r <- compare_structures(f, structures, starts = 10, cores = 8, reasoning = "Benchmark")
  r$structure[1]
}, character(1))
table(winners)
